newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian military exercise not aimed at China.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian military exercise not aimed at China.

text.p: Military exercises on a remote gas-rich island in the South China Sea are not intended as a show of force to counter China's claims in the area, Indonesia's armed forces chief said.

The exercises at Tanjung Datuk on Natuna Island, about 1,100 km (680 miles) north of Jakarta, peaked on Saturday with a sea and airborne assault on a peninsula where a multibillion gas project will be built.

"Always when our government is planning projects, the projects must be secure and investors must feel safe," armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung said while observing the 12-day exercise, which ends on Thursday.

Indonesia's military has denied the aim of the exercise, involving 19,525 personnel from all services including police, 54 aircraft and 27 warships, is to warn China over its vast claims in the South China Sea.

While Indonesia's claim to the island is undisputed, China has claimed areas which fall inside Jakarta's 320 km (200 mile) exclusive economic zone around the islands that are rich in marine life and whose seabed holds significant gas reserves.
"This is not a show of force," Tanjung said.
He also said he had been told there was no problem from Beijing's side about the military exercise.

Juwono Sudarsono, a political analyst and deputy governor of the official National Reselience Institute, played down speculation the exercises related to China's aggressive territorial claims over the Spratly and Paracel islands.
Jakarta recently questioned a Chinese maritime map that showed the Natunas as part of China's territory but accepted an explanation from Beijing saying they belonged to Indonesia.
"It is not a direct response to the perceived so-called threat of China. It just happens that we wanted to put an emphasis on seaborne landings through this exercise," Sudarsono told Reuters.
He said in the next century access to energy resources would be the key issue for regional and economic security.

A Jakarta-based foreign military attache observing the exercises, which involved a landing by a battalion of marines as well as a similar-sized paratroop unit, said the gas project was an obvious rationale for choosing the site of the operation.
"The gas is the obvious reason for choosing the site, but what is not clear is, from who are the gas reserves being defended?" the attache said.

In 1994, Indonesia signed a multibillion dollar deal with U.S.-based Exxon Corp to exploit the Natuna gas fields around the islands which contain an estimated 210 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of gas. Only 45 tcf are thought to be recoverable.
Indonesia's state-owned oil company Pertamina owns 24 percent of the Natuna project, Mobil Corp 26 percent and Exxon 50 percent. Gas from the field is expected to start flowing by 2003/2004.

Sudarsono said it was also important for the Indonesian military, in particular the navy, to practice in the region because it was of vital importance. More than 70 percent of inter-regional shipping passes through the South China Sea.
A number of foreign military attaches were invited to witness the exercises but China's representative was absent.
